processes.description: Contract administrators handle requests from shippers and desks to set up, amend, assign or terminate transport contracts: raising MDQ or TQ on an amendment, assigning a contract to another party, sending termination letters. Requests are submitted to CAS for capacity approval, credit approval is requested, and amendments are routed for signature, executed and returned. The Global Contracts system is updated, and administrators circulate contract status reports, assignment, termination and expiration reports, and contract usage files on request.
steps: A shipper or internal desk asks for a new contract, an amendment to volumes or points, an assignment or a termination.
The administrator submits the request to CAS for capacity approval and requests credit approval.
The amendment or termination letter is prepared and routed for signature.
The counterparty executes and returns the documents, and the contract is set up or updated in Global Contracts.
The approval and the contract number are confirmed back to the requester.
Contract status reports and assignment, termination and expiration reports are circulated, and contract files are pulled on request.

stalls.summary: Requesters lose track of a contract in transit and have to ask for its status because nobody is sure who has possession of it.
Amendments sit pending because the executed copies have not been returned to the administrator.
Requests and reports are revised after they are sent: a shipper corrects its own assignment request, volumes on a pending amendment are raised again, and a monthly report revision runs late.
A contract expected to move to new parties has not been transferred, and the reader is redirected to a named contact to sort it out.

contradictions.summary: The same PPL EnergyPlus contract is cited under two contract numbers with transposed digits, once when amendments are routed and again when a later amendment is signed and returned.

automation.approach: A contract request tracker fed from CAS and Global Contracts could log each request with its capacity and credit approvals, routing and signature status, and produce the contract status and assignment, termination and expiration reports from the same records instead of compiling them by hand. A checklist per request type keeps every approval and the return of executed copies from being missed.
automation.rationale: Each round repeats the same approvals and routing in the same order, and the stalls come from lost possession of contracts, unreturned signatures and late revisions. A checklist that travels with each request makes the current holder and the next step plain, and a tracker lets the status reports come from records rather than being rebuilt.

work_estimate.rationale: Most of a round goes to the system and document work behind the emails: entering or amending the contract in Global Contracts, submitting capacity approval in CAS and requesting credit approval, drafting the amendment or termination letter, and checking executed copies. That is about 30 minutes for a routine amendment, 15 for a simple approval; status reports or files of alternate-point usage push a round toward 75. Approval submissions and drafting from templates could be tool-driven; review and signature stay manual.

processes.description: Operations accounting sets the monthly allocation percentages that spread Texas Operations costs across cost centers and asks managers to review the plan allocations and update the shared spreadsheet. Managers review the charges and labor distribution on their RC reports, flag employees or purchases charged to the wrong RC, and ask for corrections. New RCs are set up to capture particular costs such as computer purchases and training, and requests for labor distribution reports are routed through a single contact.
steps: Accounting sends the monthly allocation of Texas Operations costs across cost centers as a spreadsheet.
Managers review the plan allocations and send back changes to be applied to the spreadsheet.
The corrected allocation for the month is issued.
Managers review charges and labor distribution on their RC reports and check that staff and purchases sit in the proper RC.
Misallocated people or charges are reported and correction requests are sent.
New RCs are set up for specific cost types and the basis of a charge is explained to managers.

stalls.summary: The shared allocation spreadsheet resists edits: a column cannot be inserted, so the change is abandoned and sent as a request for someone else to update.
A recipient of a correction request does not understand what is being asked, so the request has to be explained again.
Staff do not know whom to ask for a labor distribution report until a single contact is named for them.

automation.approach: A standard allocation template with fixed cost-center columns and protected formulas, plus a monthly exception report listing employees and charges whose RC differs from the expected mapping, could replace the manual line-by-line scan of RC and labor distribution reports and the rebuilding of the allocation spreadsheet.
automation.rationale: The recurring friction is the allocation spreadsheet itself and the manual scan of RC reports for misplaced people and purchases. A template that accepts changes without restructuring, paired with a mapping check, addresses both while managers still decide the corrections.

work_estimate.rationale: A round involves preparing or updating the Texas Operations allocation spreadsheet, reviewing plan allocations, or scanning an RC or labor distribution report for misplaced people and charges and working out the correction. About 30 minutes covers a typical review or allocation update, 15 a single misallocated charge; restructuring the spreadsheet or setting up a new RC reaches 60. The mapping check and spreadsheet layout could be tool-driven; choosing the right RC stays with people.

processes.description: A round starts when an invoice, payment, statement or ISO charge does not match what is booked: a counterparty bills a different price, a payment arrives that nobody can explain, a deal cannot be found in Sitara, or a capacity payment or congestion award looks wrong. Analysts search Sitara, back-track to purchase invoices and confirmation sheets, ask traders to verify pricing, correct deals, and decide whether to pay, hold or dispute the charge. Disputes are not to be raised with customers by email.
steps: An invoice, statement, payment or ISO settlement arrives that differs from the deal as booked.
The analyst looks up the deal in Sitara and compares price, volume and days with the confirmation and purchase invoices.
The trader or scheduler is asked to verify the price or explain the deal, such as a washout or a purchase to reverse.
The deal is corrected in Sitara, or the counterparty is asked to rebill at the confirmed price.
For power, ISO and PMA charges, capacity payments and congestion awards are checked against bids and schedules.
Unsupported charges are held from payment or disputed, and corrected billing is sent on.

stalls.summary: Analysts wait on traders, schedulers and counterparties to confirm prices or change the system, and send follow-ups asking whether anything was found.
Nobody is sure who handles a deal, an invoice or a billing, so items are forwarded to whoever might know, and an absence goes unnoticed while an item waits.
Sitara is not updated or holds conflicting prices, and no deal can be found for an invoiced amount, so the system has to be researched and corrected before settlement.
Information arrives late from the Hub, and ISO published prices do not match the bids, so charges cannot be settled until they are checked.

Old items resurface: an invoice for gas from months earlier that was never paid, purchase deals from a prior year still under research, and last year's incentive and service sheets to be gone through.

contradictions.summary: Counterparty invoices and confirmation sheets carry prices that differ from the deals as booked, and one counterparty changes its price again in the middle of the discussion.
Sitara holds two different prices for the same day on one deal.
Counterparty records disagree with the booked position: a counterparty's accountant does not show deals that are booked, and another counterparty cannot say why it received a payment.
ISO prices published for a congestion schedule do not match the bids submitted, and a capacity payment is questioned against the minimum rate expected for each hour.

automation.approach: An automated match of incoming invoices, statements and ISO settlement lines against Sitara deals could flag each price, volume or day mismatch with the confirmation alongside, and route the exception to the deal's owner from a maintained owner list. Analysts would then work only the flagged differences, with a standard discrepancy request carrying the deal number, days, invoiced price and booked price.
automation.rationale: Most rounds repeat the same lookups and comparisons, and the commonest stalls are waiting on replies and not knowing who owns a deal. A written procedure naming owners by counterparty and meter, the order of checks, when to hold payment, and that disputes are not emailed to customers addresses those directly, while the matching report removes the manual search.

work_estimate.rationale: A round goes to research rather than email: finding the deal in Sitara, back-tracking to purchase invoices and confirmation sheets, comparing prices day by day, correcting the deal, and for power settlements going through ISO charges, schedules and service sheets. A single price check takes about 20 minutes; a typical discrepancy with research and correction about 45; multi-month or ISO reconciliations reach 120. Matching and variance flagging could be tool-driven; deciding disputes stays with people.
